newsitem.title: LEBANON: Lebanese security says not holding Japanese.
newsitem.headline: Lebanese security says not holding Japanese.

text.p: Lebanese security forces are not holding Japanese citizens despite Lebanese and Japanese officials saying Lebanon had arrested suspected Japanese Red Army members, security sources and a government minister said.

The sources said on Monday neither the army nor army intelligence held Japanese suspects. Interior Minister Michel al-Murr said on Sunday neither the state security organ nor other organs reporting to his ministry, like internal and general security, held any Japanese.

Lebanese Foreign Minister Faris Bouez said last Tuesday Lebanese security forces had arrested Japanese citizens suspected of belonging to the Red Army guerrilla group and they were being interrogated.
Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said in Tokyo the same day that Lebanese authorities have arrested up to six key members of the Red Army in eastern Lebanon's Syrian-controlled Bekaa Valley.
Some 35,000 Syrian troops stationed over two thirds of Lebanon make Damascus Beirut's main power broker.

Murr, asked about the reported arrests, told Beirut's MTV private television station on Sunday night: "The security organs belonging to my ministry, meaning general security, internal security and airport security, have no news and have not informed me of anything."
He added: "The (state security) organ has informed me in writing that it was not holding Japanese detainees and has not interrogated them."

The Japanese premier said he had been informed by Lebanese officials that the ageing guerrillas and three supporters, all of them Japanese, were arrested in the Bekaa where they had been holed up for years.
Hashimoto has said the arrested Red Army members included 49-year-old Kozo Okamoto, a gunman involved in the 1972 Lod airport massacre in Israel. He was released by Israel in a prisoner swap in 1985.

The Red Army, founded in 1971, is allied to hardline anti-Israeli Palestinian factions. The Bekaa Valley was a haven during Lebanon's 1975-90 civil war for guerrilla groups including Lebanese Moslems and Marxists, Palestinians, Kurds and the Japanese Red Army.
